opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so a lot of my earlier work was on joint-embedding methods, things like MSN, Masked Siamese Networks, which sit in that family of invariance-based approaches. You take an image, create a couple of views of it through hand-crafted data augmentations like random crops, color jitter, blurring, and then train the network so that those views map to similar representations. That works remarkably well, especially for semantic tasks like ImageNet classification, and in the low-shot regime it was really strong.

But over time a few things started to bother me. First, those augmentations encode a lot of prior knowledge that we, as researchers, are injecting. They're tuned for images, and specifically for the kinds of downstream tasks we evaluate on. If you care about something like color or fine spatial detail, the invariances you've baked in can actually throw that information away. And it's not obvious how to transfer that recipe to other modalities like video or audio, where you'd have to design a whole new set of augmentations.

On the other side, you had generative or reconstruction-based approaches, like masked autoencoders, which don't need those hand-crafted augmentations. You just mask out parts of the input and predict the missing pixels. That's more general, but predicting in pixel space forces the model to spend capacity on low-level details that are often unpredictable or irrelevant, and the representations you get tend to need more fine-tuning to be useful for semantic tasks.

So JEPA, the Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture, felt like it captured the best of both. Like masked modeling, you're predicting missing parts of the input from context, so you don't rely on those hand-crafted view augmentations. But like joint-embedding methods, the prediction happens in representation space rather than pixel space. The model can choose to abstract away details that aren't predictable and focus on the higher-level structure. With I-JEPA, we saw that we could get strong semantic representations, competitive with the invariance-based methods, while also doing better on lower-level tasks like object counting and depth prediction, and it was significantly more compute efficient.

There was also a bigger-picture motivation. This connects to Yann's vision of building world models: systems that learn to predict how the world evolves, not in every pixel detail but in an abstract representation space. Predicting in latent space felt like the right principle for that, and images were a nice clean testbed before moving on to video, which is where we went next with V-JEPA.

r001.rationale: It says earlier methods rely on hand-crafted augmentations tuned for images and explains that a different recipe would be needed for video or audio, motivating a more general approach.

r002.rationale: It describes predicting missing input parts from context in representation space, conveying prediction of one encoded signal from another related signal.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so maybe it's worth taking a step back. A lot of my earlier work, things like PAWS and MSN, was in the family of what you'd call joint-embedding or invariance-based methods. The basic recipe is you take an image, you make two augmented views of it, random crops, color jitter, and so on, and you train the network so that the representations of those two views end up close together. And that works really well for things like ImageNet classification. But there were a couple of things that kept nagging at me.

The first is that the whole approach is built on hand-crafted augmentations. You're essentially encoding a prior about what the model should be invariant to. Color doesn't matter, scale doesn't matter, horizontal flips don't matter. And that's fine for object recognition, but it's a very specific bias. If you move to a task where color or position actually carries the semantics, or you move to another modality like video or audio where it's not even obvious what the right augmentations are, the recipe kind of falls apart. So it felt like we were leaning on a crutch rather than learning something general about the data.

The second thing is the signal itself. With invariance-based methods you're really only asking the model to learn what's shared between views. You're not asking it to understand the structure of the image, how one part relates to another. On the other side, you had masked autoencoders, which do have that nice predictive flavor, hide part of the input and reconstruct it. But they reconstruct at the pixel level, and pixels are full of information that's essentially unpredictable noise. So the model spends a lot of its capacity modeling texture and low-level detail, and you end up needing a heavy fine-tuning stage to get semantic features out of it.

JEPA, the way Yann framed it, was attractive because it sits right in between. You keep the predictive, masked formulation, you take some context from an image and predict the missing part. But you make the prediction in representation space rather than pixel space. So the target isn't the raw patch, it's the embedding of that patch from a target encoder. That lets the model decide what's worth predicting and what's not. It can drop the unpredictable details and focus on the higher-level content. And critically, there are no hand-crafted augmentations in the loop. The only thing you're doing is masking, which is a very generic operation that transfers to any modality.

So when we built I-JEPA, what I found compelling was that you could get semantic features comparable to or better than the invariance-based methods without the augmentation prior, and you were also way more compute-efficient than pixel reconstruction. And that to me pointed at something more fundamental. If the goal is to learn an internal model of the world, you want a learning signal that's about predicting abstract structure, not about reproducing every detail, and not about baking in our assumptions of what matters. JEPA was the first formulation where I felt like all of those pieces lined up.

r001.rationale: The response says earlier methods relied on hand-crafted image augmentations that encode specific invariance assumptions, and motivates JEPA as a more general approach that can transfer across modalities.

r002.rationale: The response describes using image context to predict the missing part in representation space: the target is the missing patch’s embedding from a target encoder.

astra-6.text:
What appealed to me about JEPA was the idea that we could learn by predicting in a representation space, without having to predict every detail of the image.

With image reconstruction, if you hide a patch and ask the model to predict the pixels, there’s a lot of uncertainty. The exact texture or lighting might be impossible to infer from the surrounding context, and those details may not matter for understanding what’s in the scene. Predicting a representation gives us a way to focus on more meaningful structure.

It also offered a different approach from learning representations by making two augmented views of an image agree. Those approaches depend quite a bit on how you construct the views and which transformations you decide should leave the representation unchanged. With JEPA, the question becomes: can you use one part of an image to predict a representation of another part? That felt like a promising learning signal for capturing relationships between objects and their context.

Of course, predicting representations introduces its own challenge: the model could learn to output the same thing everywhere. So the interesting part is making that prediction task work without collapse, while allowing the representations themselves to become useful.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts JEPA with image reconstruction and augmented-view methods, but it does not identify those methods’ image-specific inductive biases as the motivation for a more general learning framework.

r002.rationale: It describes using one part of an image to predict a representation of another part, conveying prediction between related image signals in representation space.

sol-6.1.text:
The motivation was really to learn representations that capture the underlying structure of an image without having to reconstruct every pixel. With contrastive approaches, a lot of that learning depends on the augmentations you choose. You create two views of an image and tell the model they should have similar representations, but those choices also determine what information the model learns to ignore.

JEPA offers a different way to formulate the problem. Given one part of an image, can you predict the representation of another part? You’re predicting in a learned representation space, so you don’t necessarily have to account for every detail of texture or lighting, as you would when predicting pixels. The hope was that this would encourage the model to learn more semantic structure, with less dependence on handcrafted augmentations. That felt like a promising foundation for learning more general models of the world.

r001.rationale: It says the earlier contrastive approach depended on image augmentations that shaped what the model learned to ignore, and presents reduced dependence on handcrafted augmentations as a path toward more general world models.

r002.rationale: It describes predicting the representation of one image part given another, but does not say that the input part is encoded before being used to predict the other part’s encoding.
